content:
Hey there, greetings.
Ive worked in the last weeks on some number theory research (please do not hit on me: Heavy LLM-Assisted) and in order to overcome scepticism and prove my work is valueable, ive implemented the proves in LEAN. Now for that i needed some more tools that were not yet available - i think they be a nice addition to mathlib and want to make a PR for them.
You can have a look at the official documentation.

You may benefit from reading the contribution guide, especially the part about AI use. The TLDR is that while everyone is happy you want to contribute, the odds that heavily LLM generated code will get into mathlib are pretty slim as of today. (Modulo how much money you spent ; )

Thanks!
Yes.. im fully aware of the scepticism regarding LLM usage. i tried my very best (im a Software Engineer) to address all of the possible problems that arrive from that. The implementation of my theorems in Lean was one of the things i did because i got a lot of scepticism about my work. Just want to make an ideal scientific rigor here - such that my work can be digested by people who really understand it easily. As Software Engineer my approach was naturaly test-driven. Extensive numerical tests before deducting any theorems. ofcourse this is not really something in number theory - thus the LEAN implementation.

For anybody interested: i also did a Case Study about my LLM-Assisted Process to make it reproduceable - and did a Research Template from it. I think this is very interesting to professional mathematicians. happy to share it to those interested.

The AI use section of the contribution guide isn't particularly about skepticism -- definitely do make sure you read it carefully and understand your PR is highly likely to be closed if it is at the quality level typically produced by LLMs.

i do not think quality is an issue.
if somebody could take a look before i do a PR, id be glad.

Im very transparent, because i like to work very clean academically here - in my view thats what heavy LLM-Assisted research needs to do in 2026 to be viable.

https://github.com/gewure/ulamnd/tree/main/research/lean/upstream/pr

Just glancing at some of the proofs (e.g., https://github.com/gewure/ulamnd/blob/main/research/lean/upstream/files/AbelSummationDiscrete.lean), it seems like they would need substantial work to be ready for mathlib. This would require significant reviewer investment, which would be better spent on human-generated PRs where the human contributor can learn from the review process.

in defensio: they line up 100% with my numerical tests in python
I think in general.. i did a really kind of big trow here and discovered previously unknown phenomenon in number theory.
What i did wrong here: the arithmetics are beyond my ability to judge it. Im a Softwareengineer - if i do not understand something, i write a test and make sure the thing i do not understand is at least proven correct :)

I know there is a ton of cranks producing complete worthless spam with LLMs in sheer unbearable amounts and overloading the ability of the Maths community to do quality control. As an amateur _recreational_ number theorist, i did just have a curious question on my mind for quite some years - and had 2 weeks without a project - decided to give this a deep dive and see what is possible with frontier models. I am myself very surprised by the outcomes.

I had one fairly simple question that nobody really raised before:

the singular series of a polynominal is somewhat well understood - Bateman-horn constant C(f) - density of primes from polynomes is known (everything fully conditional on Hardy-Littlewood, of course, as sidenote).

But what about the pair singular series? Nobody has analyzed that so far. That is paper I: and exact identity: a Dedekind Zeta function governs it.

As so many, my initial intuition was very trivial: diagonals on the Ulam spiral. Thats also where the names stems from Ulamnd. just started as a workbench to visualize/try to visualize some pseudo-patterns in the Ulam.

Why i think my process is significantly better than what people are able to do currently: as Softwareengineer i look at this completely different: Test-Driven.

I made a strong guardrailed process for AI, forced it to do numerical tests for each and every step - research Literature critically inbetween, come up with viable pathways where to do experiments and kept rigorously track of the whole process - what ideas failed, what ideas succeeded. I personaly mostly directed the paths - telling where to experiment next.

i would be extremely glad if somebody with qualification to really judge this could look into it. Not necessarily just the LEAN - but the whole research programme.

To date i published the Papers as Preprint on Zenodo as i lack an access to ArXiv. It was adversarialy attacked by some people outside the field - utilizing Frontier models to find mistakes - but everything held so far.

i am myself big time impressed about the outcome. I think this is very valueable work for the experts in this field - and especially interesting is my process.

https://zenodo.org/records/23024269

Here is my Case Study. In the Repository i have a /researchtemplate for whoever wants to reproduce the process.

Please also consider the paragraph

When reviewing PRs, we are particularly concerned that the pedagogical value of the reviewers work is wasted if there is not a human contributor actively learning.

so, beyond quality code, a question that reviewers might ask themselves (and I certainly do) is whether reviewing the PR only leads to new nice, or even beautiful, code; or to someone improving their own knowledge of Lean.
